headline: Starship lands its upper stage as AI's plumbing faces scrutiny
paragraphs: SpaceX caught the Starship upper stage, Ship 42, with the chopstick arms of its Starbase tower on Nov. 14, 2026, about 22.5 hours after liftoff — the first time an orbital rocket's upper stage has returned to its launch site and been caught, according to the company. The ship reached orbit, deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites and used three camera-carrying satellites to inspect its heat shield; SpaceX said the images looked good enough to skip a backup splashdown before the ship fired its engines after roughly 14 orbits to reenter. The same launch also produced a miss: Super Heavy aborted its own catch attempt. That pairing — a first for the upper stage, a scrub for the booster — is the honest state of reuse: demonstrated, not yet routine, and dependent on inspection data SpaceX itself vouched for.

The loudest thread across today's stories is that the physical layer of AI is now something governments and shareholders want to audit. Malaysia plans to require data-center operators to disclose AI accelerator imports, power consumption, facility locations and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers, under a law aimed at detecting GPUs diverted to export-restricted countries such as China; the Digital Ministry is still reviewing whether existing legislation lets authorities act against re-exporters, and Malaysia has approved 117 data-center projects, 55 of them operational, according to the report. In Washington, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that export controls cannot stop all restricted hardware from reaching China and that the question is whether Nvidia knew its customers were "obviously pass-through shell companies"; he said it is not known whether Jensen Huang himself knew and that he expects the board to investigate. Separately, investors Brad Gerstner of Altimeter and Gavin Baker of Atreides, holding a combined $2.13 billion in Nvidia stock, reportedly asked the board to weigh all options for leadership, including what they call "the potential return of Jensen Huang." Trade policy, corporate accountability and boardroom politics are converging on the same company.

A second thread is about defaults. Security research on Lovable, an AI app builder, found many generated apps exposed passport details and more than 200,000 private messages through publicly shipped read-only API keys and permissive Supabase defaults — a failure of what the tool ships by default, not of the underlying model, and the report does not say how many apps were affected. Italy's privacy regulator fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) after finding it accessed Android users' photos and videos without consent or notification, an action framed around consent rather than any specific permission bypass. The same pattern runs through the infrastructure stories: Microsoft said Microsoft 365 access was fully restored after a global outage that Bloomberg described as one of its longest, with no cause given; and the FAA lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributing it to copper-to-fiber wiring work at a single remote facility and a possibly "faulty router" from contractor L3Harris — a cause he framed as likely, not confirmed. Shared dependencies and shipped settings, not model capability, are where these failures live.

Meanwhile the AI software layer is moving in two directions at once. GGML, the C tensor library under llama.cpp, tagged version 1.0.0, with release notes describing a move to formal semantic versioning, removal of deprecated APIs and added FP8 support — notes we could not confirm against the GitHub release page, and users describe steady gains rather than a leap. Runway released Praxis-1, a robot controller with open weights and source code under Apache 2.0, which the company says leads the World Action Model category on Nvidia's RoboLab-120 benchmark; the stated limit is that it cannot plan complex action sequences on its own. Anthropic, by contrast, made Claude Opus 5.5 the default on all paid plans and advised users to drop "think hard" prompts and start at Medium effort — a vendor recommendation The Decoder relays without benchmarks.

The open questions are mostly about announcements outrunning evidence, which is especially visible in energy. Masdar completed its $950 million Lockhart complex in California — 365 MW of solar with 173.7 MW of battery storage, built over about four years — while Canada announced just over $634 million for charging and a grid strategy targeting more than $50 billion to double capacity by 2050, with no construction timeline. Dongfeng Nissan opened NX7 pre-orders claiming about 198 miles of electric range at roughly $20,000; Tesla's Model Y RWD range rose 8.5% to 348 miles at $39,990 per Not a Tesla App, with no primary Tesla confirmation; and reports of a $29,990 Cybercab with $299/month self-driving are unconfirmed. Watch three things next: whether SpaceX publishes booster-catch and heat-shield data from this flight; whether Nvidia's board responds at all to the investors' letter, and whether Commerce acts on the export-control delay NPR reported on headline evidence only; and whether Malaysia's law is introduced as drafted. On the ground, watch whether Canada's charging money turns into installed chargers and whether Tesla confirms the range and Cybercab figures itself.
takeaways: SpaceX caught an orbital upper stage for the first time, but the booster's aborted catch shows reuse is still being proven flight by flight.
Nvidia is being squeezed simultaneously by export-control enforcement, a Treasury Secretary questioning its customer vetting and investors asking the board to reconsider its CEO.
Exposed default settings and single points of failure — in AI-generated apps, a Microsoft cloud service, an FAA facility — caused more concrete harm today than any model capability gap.
